name: BigQuery
oneLiner: Serverless, petabyte-scale data warehouse with decoupled storage and compute.
whatItIs: BigQuery is Google Cloud's data warehouse, and it's serverless in the fullest sense: there's no cluster to size, start or tune — you write SQL and Google runs it across thousands of machines behind the scenes. Storage and compute are fully separated, so data sits cheaply and you pay for the compute a query uses (or for reserved capacity). It scans huge tables fast, handles streaming inserts, and has built-in ML (BigQuery ML) and now generative-AI functions. For many teams BigQuery is the whole analytics platform, not just the warehouse.

inPractice.narrative: Data arrives two ways: batch files loaded from Cloud Storage, and streaming rows pushed via the Storage Write API. Analysts write SQL in BigQuery to model and aggregate it — no infrastructure to manage — and Looker or Looker Studio dashboards read straight from BigQuery. Because it's serverless, a nightly transform and an ad-hoc analyst query use the same engine with no cluster to keep warm. BigQuery is both the store and the query engine.

coreConcepts.detail: No nodes to manage. Storage is billed per GB; query compute is billed separately (per TB scanned on-demand, or via reserved slots). This separation is why it scales so transparently.
A slot is a unit of query compute. On-demand queries draw from a shared pool; editions/reservations let you buy dedicated slot capacity for predictable cost and concurrency.
Partition tables by date/integer to prune scans, and cluster by common filter columns to co-locate related rows. Together they cut bytes scanned — the main cost and speed lever.
Rows can be inserted in near-real-time and queried within seconds, so BigQuery serves both batch and fresh data without a separate system.
Train and run models (regression, clustering, time-series, and calls to Vertex/Gemini) with SQL — no data export needed for many ML tasks.
Query files in Cloud Storage (or other clouds) in place; BigLake adds fine-grained governance over those external tables.

whenToUse: A serverless analytics warehouse where you don't want to manage clusters.
Fast SQL over huge datasets for BI, reporting and exploration.
Workloads mixing batch and near-real-time streamed data.
In-warehouse ML/AI via BigQuery ML without moving data.
Spiky or unpredictable query patterns (on-demand billing scales to zero when idle).
whenNotToUse: OLTP: single-row lookups and high-frequency updates — use Cloud SQL, Spanner or Firestore.
Very high-concurrency low-latency app queries — put a serving/cache layer in front.
Frequent small point mutations to individual rows — it's scan-optimised, not row-update-optimised.
When strict, capped monthly cost is essential and queries are unbounded — use reservations, not on-demand.

keyFacts.label: Model
keyFacts.value: Serverless, columnar MPP warehouse; storage and compute separated.

keyFacts.label: Compute billing
keyFacts.value: On-demand per TB scanned, or reserved slots (Editions).

keyFacts.label: Built-in
keyFacts.value: BigQuery ML, geospatial, search, external/BigLake tables.

keyFacts.label: Ops
keyFacts.value: Nothing to provision, patch or scale.

pricingShape: Two compute models: on-demand (pay per TB scanned — scales to zero when idle, but an unbounded SELECT * is a real bill) or Editions/reservations (buy slot capacity for predictable cost and concurrency). Storage is separate and cheap, with automatic long-term discounts for untouched data. The dominant lever is bytes scanned: partitioning, clustering, selecting only needed columns, and avoiding SELECT * are what keep on-demand costs sane. Reservations plus a per-user/query bytes limit are how teams cap spend at scale.
gotchas: On-demand billing is per byte scanned, so SELECT * over a wide table is expensive even for a few rows — always project columns and filter partitions.
Streaming inserts have their own cost and quotas, and streamed data has a short buffer before it's fully optimised.
Unpartitioned/unclustered big tables scan fully every time — the top cause of surprise bills.
It's not for OLTP; frequent single-row DML is slow and can hit quota limits.
Cross-region queries and data movement have rules and costs — keep datasets and compute co-located.

equivalents.name: Amazon Redshift
equivalents.note: Provisioned clusters by default (Serverless option exists); BigQuery is serverless-first.
